title: Kalshi Adopts Independent Market Integrity Committee’s Q3 Recommendations; Partners with Martha Stewart on Insider Trading Awareness Campaign
summary: Kalshi adds risk ratings to its insider trading surveillance after a Q3 committee review and launches a Martha Stewart campaign.
body_markdown:
Kalshi today accepted the third-quarter report of its independent Market Integrity Committee and will add risk ratings to its market surveillance program. The announcement coincides with the launch of Kalshi’s new advertising campaign featuring Martha Stewart.


## **About the campaign:**


By partnering with one of America’s most recognizable figures, Kalshi aims to bring broader public attention to a fundamental principle: markets only work when everyone plays by the same rules. Stewart was never convicted of insider trading, and in the campaign she reminds users that insider trading is prohibited on Kalshi, that the exchange actively monitors for it, and that violations are referred to law enforcement. It will run across TV, digital, social, and out-of-home beginning November 17.


The campaign is inspired by Stewart’s early career as a Wall Street stockbroker before she built her business empire, and connects her attention to detail to the principles behind Kalshi as a federally regulated exchange: clear rules, fair access, and the same standards for everyone.


“When I first learned about Kalshi, I was drawn to their model of being a financial exchange, similar to the stock market, where you can trade on anything from sports to tech to real-world events, but with the core principles that I stand behind: fair and transparent exchanges and healthy incentives,” said


**Martha Stewart.**


## **About the Q3 Report:**


The


**[Committee](https://news.kalshi.com/p/kalshi-surveillance-insider-trading-prevention)**


, composed of Daniel Taylor, Professor at The Wharton School and Director of the Wharton Forensic Analytics Lab, and Lisa Pinheiro, Managing Principal at Analysis Group, presented its findings to Kalshi following a months-long review of trading data from every market category on Kalshi.


It found that markets representing about 98% of trading volume carry lower risk of access to material nonpublic information, including many with publicly observable outcomes such as live sports, weather, and crypto prices. For the remaining markets, it recommended tailored alert thresholds and market-specific calibration. The result is a complex, data-driven surveillance system that operates on market-specific characteristics.


In addition to rolling out new market integrity measures, Kalshi disclosed it had made more than 50 referrals to law enforcement for suspected insider trading in Q2 and Q3.


“The value of Kalshi’s Market Integrity Committee’s work cannot be overstated,” said


**Robert DeNault, Head of Enforcement at Kalshi.**


“This is the first independent, expansive analysis of internal trading data in the prediction market space, and our team has derived tremendous value from the Committee’s insights. Our comprehensive surveillance program will now feature market-specific calibrations, allowing us to zero in on bad behavior faster and with higher priority.”


“Kalshi gave us anonymized trading data and asked us to independently analyze trading activity on the exchange; independently identify potentially suspicious trading patterns; and to help them improve their existing market surveillance systems and processes,” said


**Daniel Taylor**


, the


**Director of the Wharton Forensic Analytics Lab**


. “As an expert in data-driven enforcement, and algorithms to detect insider trading and market manipulation, I was impressed by the extent of overlap between the cases of suspicious trading that the Committee independently identified and the cases that Kalshi’s enforcement teams had already investigated, taken action against, or referred to the CFTC. I am not aware of any other CFTC-registered exchange that has provided its trading data to outside experts for independent surveillance and review.”


“Prediction markets cover a broad range of events, each with distinct characteristics and information dynamics,” said


**Lisa Pinheiro**


,


**Managing Principal at Analysis Group**


. “Even markets within the same broad category can differ substantially in their trading activity and the potential availability of material nonpublic information. Our work with Kalshi has focused on developing tailored, data-driven surveillance approaches that account for these differences, allowing for more targeted review of potentially suspicious trading activity.”


## **About the analysis**


The Committee's review covered:


-


500 million historical trades;


-


nearly 900,000 surveillance alerts;


-


over 44 billion order book updates used to reconstruct historical order books;


-


288 million recent trades representing $48 billion in volume;


-


and 5,585 market series across 421 subcategories, with refinements proposed for 21 subcategories containing mixed risk profiles.


**Assessing market categories.**


Traditional exchanges typically apply uniform surveillance algorithms by typology (insider trading, spoofing, front-running) across all products. That approach falls short for prediction markets, because while all markets trade using similar contracts and design, the underlying events that drive trading vary substantially from market to market.


For example:


-


Kalshi's Crypto "Pre-Market" subcategory includes markets about whether a company may launch a token, and also markets about the token's valuation at a specified time.


-


Kalshi's Elections "2028" subcategory includes markets about whether a politician will announce a presidential run, and also markets about the popular-vote margin.


These markets carry different insider trading risks. The Committee recommended grouping markets with similar characteristics so Kalshi can tailor surveillance to each group’s risk profile, rather than applying uniform parameters across broad categories like sports. Kalshi will adopt the Committee’s risk ratings and restructure these mixed subcategories accordingly.


**Calibrating alert thresholds.**


Kalshi is building a tiered surveillance algorithm based on subcategory risk levels, with thresholds calibrated from historical activity and most alert capacity directed at higher-risk markets. This will reduce false positives, focus review on higher-risk activity, and allow more retrospective analysis.


**Pairing real-time alerts with retrospective analysis.**


Alongside real-time alerts on individual trades, the Committee evaluated cross-market, longer-term measures such as account profitability and success rates. This approach could surface suspicious patterns that are not visible in a single trade or a single market, complementing real-time alerting.


**Going forward.**


The Committee will continue working with Kalshi to extend its analysis to other forms of potential manipulation, including spoofing.
